articles.title: California removed invasive rabbits from Santa Barbara Island; its endangered native dudleya stopped declining, with 534 plants later counted
articles.summary: The eradication of invasive rabbits on Santa Barbara Island has led to a remarkable recovery of the endangered Dudleya plant, with numbers surging from extinction fears to record highs.
articles.body: There are plants and creatures unique to the Channel Islands off the coast of southern California. Santa Barbara Island, about one square mile in area and home to plant species found only on the Channel Islands, illustrates the vulnerability of isolated island ecosystems. Over the course of more than a century, a large portion of its native vegetation was removed by goats, sheep, farms, and eventually rabbits.One fatality was the Santa Barbara Island liveforever, a succulent found nowhere else. Rabbits, often called hares in older accounts, chewed it so heavily that botanists feared in the early 1970s that it might be extinct. The National Park Service began removing an estimated 6,000 rabbits in 1954 and continued control efforts until the last rabbits were eliminated in 1981. The plant's decline subsequently stabilized, with 534 plants recorded around Signal Peak in 1984, 2,353 counted island-wide in 2020 and about 3,800 recorded in 2024. It remains classified as endangered.A plant on the vergeDudleya traskiae, the liveforever, has rosettes of thick, pale green leaves and produces yellow flowers from spring into early summer. It grows on steep rocky slopes and sea cliffs surrounding the rim of the island. Earlier grazing by goats and sheep, followed by introduced rabbits and hares, severely altered the island's native vegetation. In the next decades came hares and rabbits. In 1950, a biologist identified only two rabbits, but by 1953 he reported that native vegetation had been damaged almost to the extent caused by earlier sheep grazing.By April 1978, when the US Fish and Wildlife Service designated the plant as endangered, only two populations were known to exist. One showed three plants coming out from stubs eaten down by animals to ground level; the other was a few hundred plants on a sea cliff out of reach of the creatures. A later Fish and Wildlife Service assessment, citing a 1975 Smithsonian report, said the plant had not been collected since 1968 and was considered possibly extinct. The listing blamed hares, but further investigation revealed the animals were actually rabbits. Now that the grazing was finished, the question was, how many plants were left?The last rabbits left in 1981, and park workers inspected the island in 1982, 1983, and 1984, discovering eleven colonies. The cliffs at Signal Peak were the only place where more than 100 plants were found, and discoveries in 1984 increased the estimate for that region to 534, according to a Fish and Wildlife Service evaluation of the species. In a three-year study from 1985 to 1987, the plants in its sample plots were found to be virtually steady, while the overall number of rosettes increased by 22%.Subsequent estimates were low but promising, numbering 852 plants island-wide in 2004 and 928 in 2006. The assessment cautioned that such numbers depended on assumptions about the cliffs at Signal Peak, so a real increase from one year to the next couldn’t be shown. Recruitment has been a perennial issue. Deer mice eat the seeds; dryness kills the seedlings, and when park officials planted roughly 800 seedlings in 2005, just 15 per cent survived until January 2006. More recent surveys have recorded substantially higher numbers, although the assessment notes uncertainty caused by different survey methods and the difficulty of counting plants on steep terrain.Threats that remainA later Fish and Wildlife Service assessment reported that 2020 surveys counted 2,353 plants, the highest total recorded to date. Most, 1,683, were in one stand visible only in aerial photos, meaning those plants had probably been there for years and uncounted. The study found no obvious overall pattern, with some colonies expanding and others contracting or dying, and it maintained the listing as an endangered species.The rabbit problem has largely been resolved, but other pressures remain. Native deer mice devour seeds, seedlings and mature plants, and 506 young plants planted out near the island’s dwellings and campsite in July 2019 had all disappeared by 2020, likely eaten by mice. Brown pelicans can also damage rosettes and alter the soil in ways that favor grasses. The assessment also identified introduced annual grasses and iceplant, along with fire risk, as continuing pressures on the species. They increased their roosting on the island from around 2004 onwards. Introduced annual grasses and iceplants continue to dominate most of the area, boosting both competition and fire risk. Conservationists have already collected seed and grown hundreds of seedlings on an island nursery. The assessment calls for regular monitoring and protective cages for fresh plantings.The available evidence suggests the rabbit removal helped the plant recover, although it was not the only factor. The species persisted after the rabbits were eliminated, new colonies were identified and later surveys recorded substantially more plants than earlier counts. But regeneration on a small, devastated island is gradual, and the future of the plant rests on managing mice, pelicans, weeds and fire as carefully as the rabbits once were.You use AI every day. articles.title: UK arrests British-Iranian suspect over RAF ‘plot’: What we know
articles.summary: Police investigate ‘possible foreign state involvement’ as sixth man arrested over RAF Fairford incident.
articles.body:
United Kingdom police have arrested a 25-year-old British-Iranian man in relation to a security incident at a Royal Air Force (RAF) station near Fairford, England, this week

The man, described by police as a “dual UK/Iranian national” and detained on suspicion of preparing “terrorist” acts, is the sixth person to be arrested in what British authorities said was potentially an Iran-backed plot. The five other people arrested earlier were released on bail on Monday.

The investigation began when British authorities were alerted early on Sunday about unusual activity near the airbase, including oddly parked vans and a group of masked men. After searching the vans, authorities found no weapons or explosives but did recover a “quantity of petrol”.

The RAF station has been used by the United States for military operations, including by bombers during the US-Israel war on Iran.

Here’s what we know about the latest development in the case:

British counterterrorism police announced the arrest of a 25-year-old British-Iranian dual national in Westminster, London, on Thursday. Iran, however, does not recognise dual citizenship, and treats Iranians with a second passport solely as Iranian.

The man was detained on “suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006”, the same offence cited in the arrests of the five other suspects. In line with standard police practice, none of the suspects has been named ahead of any charges being made.

Police said they also conducted searches of two properties in the London area. They appealed to the public for any information that could assist the investigation.

What do we know about the suspect in custody?

The Times newspaper reported that the British-Iranian suspect is being investigated as a possible “recruiter” in the still-opaque plot or as someone otherwise believed to have played a significant role.

The media reported that the man was placed under surveillance after the arrest of the first five men. He has not been named.

What evidence is there that this was an Iran-linked plot?

The UK has pointed to an Iranian connection but has so far kept the reason for that assessment under wraps.

On Wednesday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there are “strong indications” of Iran’s involvement in the incident and an “ongoing, complex and serious police investigation” is continuing.

He did not give information on what the suspects may have been planning or what intelligence has led the UK to suspect the involvement of Iran, saying only that he would “update people more in due course”.

In the US, President Donald Trump said the case “might be” Iran-linked and the US had been keeping tabs on the suspects “for a long time”. Trump criticised the UK’s decision to release the first five suspects on bail.

In Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said his government had forewarned the UK about a potential “Iranian-sponsored attack” but did not specify if that was related to the same RAF base incident.

Iranian officials have firmly denied any connection to the incident. Deputy Foreign Minister for Political Affairs Majid Takht-Ravanch called the claims “false and ridiculous”.

Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs summoned British Ambassador Hugo Shorter on Thursday to protest against the allegations.

Authorities received two early-morning calls on Sunday alerting them to suspicious activity near the Fairford airbase, including three vans parked strangely and a group of hooded, masked men.

Unusually, the first call to the UK’s emergency line was made by one of the suspects who would later be arrested.

Police responded and arrested five British men in their early 20s in the nearby Whelford area, saying they were suspected of explosives offences. Counterterrorism police later took over the investigation and said the men were suspected of preparing “a terrorist act”.

The suspects were released on bail on Monday but remained subject to “stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others”, according to the UK’s head of counterterrorism policing, Laurence Taylor.

After searching the vans located near the airbase, police said they found no explosives but did retrieve a “quantity of petrol”.

Why were the men arrested at the scene given bail if this is a major incident?

That’s one of the big unanswered questions.

Under British “counterterrorism” law, police may hold suspects for up to two weeks before charging them. However, if authorities find little evidence to support their initial suspicion of “terrorism”, they have far less time – usually 24 to 36 hours, Chris Phillips, a former head of the UK’s National Counter Terrorism Security Office, told Al Jazeera.

Other security experts told Al Jazeera that police likely released the first five suspects because they did not deem them to be an imminent security risk or found that their potential involvement in any plot was unwitting.

“In cases involving terrorism, suspects can still be released on bail when the authorities feel relatively confident that these individuals do not pose an imminent danger of either carrying out or organising a terrorist attack,” Andrew Silke, professor of criminology at Royal Holloway, University of London, told Al Jazeera.

“Individuals may have been involved unknowingly or in a peripheral manner to potential terrorist activity. This seems possible in the current case,” he added.

Afzal Ashraf, a visiting fellow in international relations and security at Loughborough University and a former senior RAF officer, agreed that police likely have assessed that the five released suspects do not pose “any immediate danger”.

“We can reasonably assume that police judged that these individuals did not present any immediate danger nor did they have any credible means or intention of creating further danger to the public or to government installations,” Ashraf told Al Jazeera.

However, he said their release on bail should not necessarily be taken to mean the incident in question “was minor or that the Iranian-involvement hypothesis has been rejected”.

British authorities said they are continuing to investigate all aspects of the case, including the possibility of it being a foreign-backed “plot”.

Silke said authorities will likely be thoroughly analysing all suspects’ communications and interactions, looking for information on contacts who may have organised their involvement and for any payment the suspects may have received.

“The authorities can investigate all of these links to establish if they lead back to foreign government sources or agencies,” he said.

Silke added that authorities will also look into any links between the RAF airbase incident and previous plots carried out on British soil.

Phillips said he believes the suspects could have been recruited online by foreign actors to carry out some type of malicious activity, such as “setting fire to something”.

He said both Russia and Iran have allegedly paid “stooges” to carry out such acts in recent years. “At first glance now, it seems that that may be the case, but time will tell,” Phillips added.

Iran and Russia have also previously been accused of orchestrating plots in the UK. Those plots have involved “surveillance, sabotage, arson or physical violence”, MI5 Director General Ken McCallum said last year.

articles.title: Swansea toddler found in road after wandering off from Seren Fach nursery
articles.summary: Two-year-old Noah was found in the middle of a busy road in Swansea, his parents say.
articles.body:
Parents who claim their toddler wandered off from nursery and was found by a stranger on a busy road say they have been left traumatised.

Sarah, 22, and Tarik, 24, from Swansea, said their two-year-old son Noah was found on his own on Gors Avenue, Mayhill.

"He could have been hit by a car, a bus, he could have been taken," Tarik said.

Seren Fach Day Nursery said it had implemented additional safety measures and "the safety, welfare and protection" of every child in their care remained a priority.

South Wales Police said it was investigating the incident after officers responded to reports of "safeguarding concerns" when a child left nursery without the knowledge of staff.

"This stuff shouldn't be happening, especially in a safe place," Tarik said. "How is that even possible?"

Sarah added: "When you drop your children off in school or nursery you never think that anything could happen to them because they are in a professional's hands."

The couple said they had found out about the incident when they had arrived to pick Noah up from nursery about 40 minutes afterwards.

They said the nursery blamed the incident on "no-one watching him" and "a door being left open".

But Noah's parents said he would have to pass through two baby gates, four doors including fire doors, and the main gate to reach Gors Avenue.

The couple have since taken Noah out of nursery, and said several other pupils have also been withdrawn as a result of the incident.

Despite them keeping a watchful eye on Noah, they said they were fearful for his safety and cannot rest.

"It's the worst possible scenario. We can't sleep, we know he's safe, pray to God he's safe, but we keep checking in on him."

The parents said they had spoken to three eyewitnesses who claim Noah had been alone with no adult supervision, and that the nursery had been unaware he was missing.

"When we first got in, we spoke to the manager, who said they were very sorry and there was no excuse for the doors to be open," Tarik said.

The nursery then made the couple aware of posts on Facebook about the incident, including a post from Nicolle Richards, who said she found Noah in the middle of the road and reported the incident.

In the post, Richards said: "Today has been one of the scariest days of my life. I was driving up Gors Avenue and could see a little boy walking in the middle of the road.

"I stopped and grabbed him, a man went down to the nursery to grab someone, a woman come out I explained he was in the middle of the road."

"We drop him off to nursery and think he's in a safe place. It's scary, the fact our son was in the middle of the road on his own," Tarik said.

"The police aren't taking it lightly, this is a two-year-old. We took Noah out of nursery as soon as it happened.

"[Sarah] hasn't been sleeping. We just keep checking."

In a statement on Facebook, Seren Fach Day Nursey said it was aware of the post on social media and "completely understand why members of the public and our families are concerned after reading the post".

It said: "The safety and wellbeing of the children entrusted to our care is something we take incredibly seriously, and we would never seek to minimise a concern of this nature.

"Seren Fach Day Nursery has been part of the local community for over 30 years and during that time we have cared for generations of children and families.

"We have established safeguarding and security procedures in place, alongside staff training and risk assessments, all of which are being carefully investigated as part of our response to this incident.

"We would ask that people avoid speculation or sharing information about the child or those involved on social media.

"Please raise any concerns directly with the nursery or the relevant authorities so that they can be properly addressed."

Care Inspectorate Wales (CIW) said it was unable to comment while inquiries were ongoing, but it would take "any necessary action" to ensure children's safety and wellbeing.

"Where concerns are raised, we work to ensure providers meet the national minimum standards for regulated childcare, which include specific requirements on safeguarding, premises security and child protection.

"We would encourage anyone with concerns about the care of a child to contact CIW directly."

articles.title: In 2015, Utah man Cory Mohl began building a backyard railroad; after 40,000 pounds of gravel and hundreds of hours, neighbours were riding it and he expected a final cost near $18,000
articles.summary: In 2015, Cory Mohl of West Valley City, Utah, turned a lifelong fascination with trains into a full-scale backyard project.
articles.body: In 2015, Cory Mohl of West Valley City, Utah, turned a lifelong fascination with trains into a full-scale backyard project. Over the next several months he laid about 400 feet of track, hauled roughly 40,000 pounds of gravel for the roadbed, and invested hundreds of hours of labour into what he jokingly calls the Cory Mohl Railroad. By mid-2016 the line was complete, neighbourhood children were asking for rides, and Mohl told ABC News he expected the final cost to land near $17,500 to $18,000. Read on to know more about Mohl and his unusual idea here:A childhood love that never fadedMohl, then 43, described himself as a lifelong train enthusiast who had spent years building and storing model railroads.He told ABC News that he had always wanted to return to the hobby in a bigger way once his daughter was older and more independent. When the idea of a backyard railroad took hold in December 2015, he said he simply got a wild bug and decided to do it, turning a personal passion into a tangible, rideable creation.The project gave him a chance to revisit the joy he felt as a child around trains, but on a scale that friends and neighbours could experience directly. Instead of watching a miniature locomotive circle a tabletop layout, people could sit in a small car and travel along a real track that wound through his yard and even into a shed.For Mohl, the backyard railroad was both a personal milestone and a way to share his enthusiasm with the community around him.Building a real railroad on a residential lotThe Cory Mohl Railroad stretches about 400 feet around the yard, not counting the sections that run through the shed. Laying that much track required careful planning to fit the line into a typical residential lot while still offering a satisfying ride. Mohl moved roughly 40,000 pounds of gravel to create a stable roadbed, then set the rails, ties, and switches by hand over many weekends and evenings, as per the report.He sourced the locomotive from another local enthusiast who lived about half a mile away and already had a railroad that ran around his house and across his driveway. That connection made it easier for Mohl to acquire equipment that was designed for backyard use and compatible with the scale of track he was installing. The purchase helped him avoid the cost and complexity of building a custom engine from scratch.Hundreds of hours and a growing price tagMohl estimated that he spent hundreds of hours on the project between planning, earthmoving, track laying, and finishing work. Each stage demanded attention to detail, from grading the ground so the train would run smoothly to ensuring the track was level and properly aligned. The labour was largely unpaid, but the time investment was a major part of what made the railroad feel like a true passion project rather than a simple weekend upgrade.As materials and equipment added up, Mohl tracked his spending and told ABC News he expected the final cost to settle around $17,500, with some reports rounding that figure to nearly $18,000. That amount covered track, gravel, the locomotive, rolling stock, and various supplies needed to make the line safe and functional. For a backyard hobby, the price was substantial, but Mohl viewed it as the cost of building something unique and enduring.Neighbours line up for ridesOnce the railroad was operational, it quickly became a local attraction. Mohl said a few people started coming by to ask about the setup, and children in the neighbourhood began requesting rides. The sight of a small train circling a residential yard was unusual enough to draw attention, but the chance to actually ride it turned the project into a shared experience for families on the block.Those rides transformed the railroad from a private hobby into a community feature. Parents could watch their children climb into a car and travel along the track, while Mohl operated the train and explained how the system worked. In that sense, the backyard railroad became a social space as much as a technical achievement, creating moments of connection between neighbours who might not otherwise interact.Plans to expand and decorateEven with the main line complete, Mohl had ideas for making the railroad more elaborate. He said he intends to expand the track even more and add decorations for the upcoming holidays. These additions might include seasonal themes or lights or small structures along the route, all of which are intended to enhance the experience of riders and viewers alike. These expansions would be a continuation of what he had already created, making the railroad an evolving project rather than a one-time build. Each new section or decoration would be a reflection of his ongoing passion for trains and his desire to keep putting time and money into the hobby. The railroad, for Mohl, was never meant to be static, but rather a living manifestation of his childhood dream.Why backyard railroads capture people's imaginationBackyard railroads exist in a unique space between model train layouts and full-size heritage lines. They’re big enough to ride on and operate like real trains, but small enough to fit on private property and be maintained by one enthusiast or family. This middle road allows builders to combine engineering, landscaping and storytelling in a way that appeals to both adults and children. Mohl’s project demonstrates how a personal passion can bleed into the public realm, even within the confines of a residential yard. The Cory Mohl Railroad became a source of pride for the neighborhood, and a physical reminder that large-scale creativity is still possible in suburban settings. articles.title: In 1992, California finished removing feral goats from San Clemente Island; a rare native plant later rebounded to more than 3,500 individuals
articles.summary: The successful removal of feral goats from San Clemente Island led to a remarkable recovery of the endangered San Clemente Island paintbrush, showcasing the potential for ecological restoration and species revival.
articles.body: On San Clemente Island, off the coast of Southern California, an unlikely conservation story unfolded after one of the island's most damaging pressures was finally removed. Feral goats had grazed across the island for generations, stripping vegetation, trampling the ground, and causing erosion. Among the plants affected was the San Clemente Island paintbrush (Castilleja grisea), a small perennial found nowhere else.According to Annals of Botany, by the time the goats and other non-native grazing animals had been removed in the early 1990s, the San Clemente Island paintbrush had become extremely rare. Once grazing pressure ended, the plant began reappearing in areas where it had been difficult to find. Surveys in the late 1990s recorded more than 3,500 individuals, consistent with a substantial recovery after goat removal.How grazing reshaped the islandSan Clemente Island had been extensively used by livestock for many years. Sheep, cattle, pigs, and goats had been brought to the island, and the grazing practices over decades damaged the native vegetation. In addition to eating vegetation, the livestock trampled plants and carved trails that contributed to soil erosion. The goats were difficult to remove because they could survive in the island’s rugged terrain and hide in inaccessible areas.According to the Santa Barbara Botanic Garden, the US Navy began an organised feral-goat eradication programme in 1972, working with other organisations to remove goats from San Clemente Island over the following decades. As the population became smaller and more difficult to locate, the programme later used the "Judas goat" technique, in which radio-collared goats helped researchers find groups of goats that remained in remote areas. Between 1989 and 1991, 263 goats were killed during this later phase of the eradication effort. By 1992, the remaining non-native ungulates had been removed from the island, ending decades of grazing pressure on its native vegetation.The paintbrush begins to returnThe San Clemente Island paintbrush was once fairly common, but intensive grazing sharply reduced its numbers. In 1977, it was placed on the federal endangered species list. By the late 1970s, only a few plants were known to remain. But the situation changed once the goats disappeared from the scene. Research published in Annals of Botany also notes that the plant began to rebound after the goats were removed, with more than 3,500 individuals counted in the late 1990s. Scientists studying the plant’s genetics noted fairly high genetic diversity despite its long period of scarcity.Surveys in 1996 and 1997 recorded 77 populations and about 3,500 individual plants. Later surveys found even larger numbers. From 2003 to 2006, researchers recorded 198 populations containing an estimated 9,718 individual plants. Vegetation around San Clemente Island also recovered after the feral goats were eradicated, with native plants able to persist in areas that were previously exposed to heavy grazing pressure.Recovery did not mean the work was overThe removal of the goats took away one of the greatest pressures that the paintbrush faced, but it was not the only problem. The plant’s recovery took place amid concerns about soil erosion, invasive plants, fire, land use, and military activity. The US Fish and Wildlife Service has noted that some of the plant's current distribution may reflect areas where steep terrain once protected it from goats. Seeds may also have remained in the soil, allowing the species to recolonise areas after grazing ended. This suggests the recovery had multiple contributing factors, though removing non-native herbivores addressed the primary threat identified when the plant was listed.Nevertheless, the plant’s recovery was strong enough to prompt a change in its legal status. The San Clemente Island paintbrush was delisted from the endangered species list in 2023. The US Fish and Wildlife Service says the species recovered after non-native herbivores were removed. Once grazing pressure ended, the plant had a chance to grow again. The plant recovered from a small number to thousands.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Ashamed': Cornell students gather to voice anger over alleged gang rape
articles.summary: Students tell the BBC that the tension on campus has become palpable since allegations from 2024 resurfaced.
articles.body:
Students have called for drastic change at Cornell University as a result of an alleged gang rape in 2024, with one using an emotional student assembly on Thursday to say: "We're absolutely ashamed of the events that happened on campus."

Students and faculty members say the investigation into the incident has cast a "dark cloud" over the campus - stirring anger, concern over fraternity culture, and a backlash against the university's handling of the situation.

At Thursday's assembly, some labelled the perceived lack of justice a "disgrace" and criticised the prestigious university, which has defended its handling of the case.

"We deserve to know that our institution values our safety more than its reputation," undergraduate Sophia Riley Sim told those at the gathering.

Sim said she had been too upset by the case to attend classes for the past week.

Under normal circumstances, the Ivy League university is a beautiful place to study at this time of year. Autumn leaves bring pops of colour to its stately buildings, which are set against the backdrop of the rolling hills of upstate New York.

But students and staff who spoke to the BBC - some on condition of anonymity - said the tension on campus had become palpable since the 2024 case resurfaced in recent weeks.

The accuser at the centre of the alleged gang rape, known anonymously as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit against Cornell on 16 September, saying she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house during the incident two years ago.

She claimed that Cornell had failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved in the incident. The men have been dubbed the Cornell Seven.

Cornell has already agreed to an independent investigation into the rape allegation.

The university has also defended its handling of the issue to date , saying it conducted an "extensive investigation" that lasted several months following the report of the incident, and that it followed applicable federal civil rights law.

Shortly after Thursday's student assembly at Cornell, New York Governor Kathy Hochul announced she had appointed the state attorney general, Letitia James, as special prosecutor in the case.

She said she had "lost faith" in the Tompkins County district attorney, who was previously leading the investigation. James therefore takes over the case from Matthew Van Houten.

Van Houten's office initially concluded that the evidence did not meet the legal threshold to bring charges - before reopening a criminal investigation last week in light of the new civil complaint, a move that Cornell supported.

Cornell accuser was 'failed' by university health care system, lawyer says

What we know about Cornell University frat house rape investigation

Cornell case highlights 'draining' maze for victims to report campus sex assaults

An upcoming "Justice for Survivors" protest, planned at the university for 5 October, is being advertised in flyers all over campus. It calls on Cornell to take action against alleged rape culture.

Student organisers are calling for Cornell to expel and revoke the degrees of the alleged perpetrators of the rape, rewrite policies around sexual assault punishments, initiate an external investigation of the university and mandate prevention training for campus police.

As part of its account of its prior investigation of the case, Cornell says: "At its conclusion, the hearing panel issued a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell."

Cornell says it is legally prevented from publicly disclosing specific disciplinary outcomes about disciplinary students, adding that "we recognise that this legal limitation can be frustrating".

Across campus, the case has stirred anger.

One fourth-year student recalled that it had been hard to live there in 2024, in the aftermath of the incident, as rumours began spreading about Jane Doe.

Now, two years on, she told the BBC how she and her friends felt "overwhelmed" and "disappointed", comparing the atmosphere on campus to a "dark cloud". Cornell, she believes, mishandled things.

She wants the administration to admit what she sees as its mistakes, calling the lack of transparency disheartening.

She also asked why multiple men in a group chat for members of Chi Phi - the fraternity group at the centre of the allegations - did not speak up. A chapter of the fraternity was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus.

Students and community members also used Thursday's student assembly meeting to vent their frustrations and disappointment.

"I am very disgusted to be here, to be paying this institution to be here," freshman Eliana Dolven-Miller said. "There was a lot of anger in that room, I was very angry."

Eeshaan Chaudhuri, the student assembly chair, opened the meeting by saying that the campus stood "with victims of sexual violence".

"We don't tolerate it here on campus, and I think I can speak for every single one of us, and I can say we're absolutely ashamed of the events that happened on our campus," Chaudhuri said.

The student group has also raised a resolution calling on the university to release a written account of how it handled the alleged sexual assault, including what evidence was gathered and whether and when the university referred the matter to campus police.

A faculty member said the mood on campus was "dismal". Staff were not trained therapists, she said, so it was hard to know how to navigate these discussions with students.

It was an "incredible situation that was so… I just don't understand," she said, adding that she was unsure if the university should have gone further, and adding that this was not the first time a fraternity group had had problems on campus.

Some of the freshmen, or first-year students, who spoke to the BBC had only arrived at Cornell last month.

A young woman said she and her friends had been discussing the allegations again that morning. Her friend said it had been difficult for him to come to an Ivy League university feeling excited about the future, only to see this story dominate the news.

Students were not OK about what happened to Jane Doe, he said.

Cornell alumni have also given their views.

More than 1,300 graduates have signed a letter calling on the university to take "swift and expansive" action after the allegations came back to light.

"Will Cornell take this as an opportunity to ask difficult questions about the proliferation of sexual violence on its own campus?" asks the letter, which was published in the university's student newspaper.

"Or will it shy away from reform to protect its image? This is not an isolated incident."

articles.title: How can Jordan respond to Israel’s escalation across the West Bank?
articles.summary: Settlement expansion, displacement and growing Israeli control would have direct consequences for Jordan.
articles.body:
It is increasingly difficult to regard what is happening in the West Bank as merely a series of measures that the Israeli government justifies on security grounds or as part of counterterrorism operations. Taken together, the cumulative pattern and expanding scope of these measures point to a broader political and territorial trajectory: one aimed at reshaping the West Bank, imposing new facts on the ground, entrenching Israeli control and advancing the de facto annexation of large parts of the territory while simultaneously subjecting Palestinians to mounting pressure that, directly or indirectly, pushes them from their land.

Israeli, journalistic and research reports have documented the intensification of this trajectory through settlement expansion, land confiscation, restrictions on Palestinian movement, control over water resources and grazing areas as well as military operations and repeated internal displacement in several parts of the West Bank.

Considered individually, each of these measures may appear to be a separate issue. Viewed together, however, they reveal a more consequential development: an effort to re-engineer the geography and demography of the West Bank in ways that undermine the prospect of establishing a contiguous and viable Palestinian state.

The question, therefore, is no longer simply what is happening in the West Bank.

The more urgent question is how can Jordan, the Palestinians, the Arab world and the international community prevent this trajectory from becoming a permanent reality.

Jordan Valley at the heart of the equation

The Jordan Valley assumes exceptional importance in this context, not only because of its geographical and security significance but also because of its agricultural and economic importance and its water resources for the Palestinian people.

Reports concerning the construction of a new Israeli barrier, referred to as the “Crimson Thread”, extending roughly 480km (300 miles) from the Golan Heights to the Red Sea, warrant serious Jordanian, Arab and international scrutiny, particularly if such a project is intended to isolate the Jordan Valley and place as much as 83 percent of its total area under Israeli control.

Such a development could in effect sever the West Bank from Jordan and deprive Palestinians of one of their most important agricultural and water resources.

Borders, walls, roads and settlements cease to be merely physical infrastructure when they are combined with control over land and water. They become instruments for reshaping political and demographic geography and weakening the ability of Palestinians to remain on their land.

This is precisely where the Palestinian issue intersects directly with Jordan’s national security.

Jordan cannot treat developments in the West Bank as an exclusively Palestinian matter. At its core, this is an issue of Jordanian national security, regional stability and the future of the Palestinian cause.

Any fundamental change to the geographical or demographic reality of the West Bank will inevitably carry direct consequences for Jordan because of geography, history and proximity. And if the eventual outcome is forced displacement, then, as King Abdullah II has repeatedly made clear, such a scenario would amount to a declaration of war on Jordan.

The policy required of Jordan at this stage, therefore, must be proactive: one that anticipates possible scenarios and prepares for them politically, diplomatically, economically and in security terms.

Jordan’s first line of defence is its national unity.

At this stage, it is essential to strengthen the concepts of citizenship and the state, consolidate full equality among Jordanians, and reject any discourse or practice that creates divisions on the basis of origin, region or roots.

The Palestinian cause must remain a national, Arab and humanitarian cause. It must not be allowed to become a source of division within Jordanian society.

Responsibility falls on both the state and society to confront hate speech and incitement, apply the law equally and fairly, and protect the national fabric from attempts to exploit regional turmoil to sow division among Jordanians.

One of the gravest outcomes Jordan must prevent is the transfer of the conflict into its own domestic sphere. Relations among Jordanians of different origins, including those of Jordanian and Palestinian heritage, must never become a vulnerable fault line through which those seeking discord, whether from within the country or from abroad, can operate.

National unity, therefore, is not merely a social value. It is an integral component of Jordan’s national security architecture.

Second: Move from diplomacy of protest to diplomacy of pressure and proportionate action

Jordan has accumulated considerable international credibility and diplomatic capital. The present phase, however, requires Jordan to expand the tools at its disposal.

It is no longer sufficient simply to condemn settlement activity, reject annexation or warn against displacement. What is needed is an Arab, Islamic and international diplomatic front capable of translating political positions into practical measures.

In coordination with Palestine and Arab and Islamic states, Jordan should work to:

Mobilise countries that reject annexation and settlement expansion.

Push for concrete measures and sanctions not only against settlements but also against state policies that enable and encourage them.

Use Arab political and economic relations with influential states more strategically, expanding economic cooperation with countries that adopt firm positions against the Israeli occupation while recalibrating engagement with those that remain reluctant to take clear positions towards Israeli policies.

Build an international coalition capable of preventing the imposition of irreversible facts by force.

A comparison with Russia’s war in Ukraine is instructive. When Russia occupied large areas of Ukrainian territory, sanctions were not confined to the territories under occupation; they were imposed on Russia itself. The question, therefore, is why a different standard should apply elsewhere.

The international community does not lack resolutions or statements. What it lacks is the conversion of political will into a tangible cost for those who violate international law.

Third: Establish an Arab and Islamic fund for Palestinian resilience

If the objective is to prevent displacement and enable Palestinians to remain on their land, financial support must become a sustained strategic policy rather than seasonal assistance tied to moments of crisis.

One option would be to establish an Arab, Islamic and international fund dedicated to strengthening Palestinian resilience with a mandate to finance specific projects in the West Bank and Gaza, including:

Protecting land threatened with confiscation.

Developing water resources and irrigation networks.

Financing housing projects in vulnerable areas.

Supporting education and health services.

Assisting municipalities and local councils.

Providing alternative sources of income to families who have lost employment as a result of Israeli measures.

Resilience is not merely a political slogan. It is a material reality.

Every Palestinian family who remains on its land, every farmer who continues to cultivate his fields and every village that retains access to its water resources represents part of the effort to prevent displacement.

Fourth: Treat the Jordan Valley as a Jordanian national security issue

Jordan should address developments in the Jordan Valley as a permanent strategic file.

A specialised Jordanian mechanism should be established to monitor:

The construction of roads, barriers and walls.

Any measures that could permanently alter the status quo.

These developments should be documented through maps, satellite imagery, statistics and official records so Jordan maintains a comprehensive dossier that can be used politically and legally before the international community.

Struggles over land are not determined by force alone. They are also shaped by documentation, maps, law and the ability to present an authoritative, evidence-based account of what is happening.

Fifth: Strengthen Jordan’s national defence architecture

Strengthening Jordan’s ability to protect its security, borders and national interests is not optional.

Jordan is a country with limited resources, but it possesses significant human and institutional expertise. It can further develop an advanced national defence, civil protection and crisis-management architecture.

This could include strengthening national service and training programmes, enhancing civil defence preparedness, protecting critical infrastructure, reinforcing cybersecurity and border security, and improving disaster and emergency management.

Jordan could also draw on the extensive experience of retired military personnel through structured national programmes under the supervision of appropriate state institutions, thereby strengthening the country’s overall defensive readiness.

The strength Jordan requires is the strength of deterrence, protection and preparedness, not an impulse towards an ill-considered confrontation.

Sixth: Prevent Jordan from becoming an “alternative homeland”

This issue must remain at the centre of Jordanian strategic calculations.

Any project that directly or indirectly leads to the depopulation of the West Bank or pushes large numbers of Palestinians towards Jordan is not merely a humanitarian question. It would carry profound political, security and demographic consequences for the kingdom.

Jordan’s position, therefore, must remain unequivocal: Resolving the Palestinian question cannot come at Jordan’s expense; displacement is not a political solution; and Jordan is not an alternative homeland for the Palestinian people.

At the same time, Jordan must preserve the humanitarian and legal dimensions of its response to any forced developments, so that opposition to displacement does not translate into further suffering for civilians.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Haiti: More than 5,000 people killed or injured due to gang violence in 2026 , UN says
articles.summary: The United Nations said violent gangs continue to "adapt and expand" across the country, further threatening its stability.
articles.body:
More than 5,700 people have been killed or injured by gangs or during operations against them between 1 January and 11 September 2026, the United Nations has said.

UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk added that more than 230 people have also been kidnapped.

An estimated 1,000 women and girls have been raped - but Türk noted that the actual figure is "likely much higher".

Gangs have been exerting varying degrees of power in Haiti for decades. The most recent widespread outbreak of gang violence has been fuelled by the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse on 7 July 2021 .

Armed men kidnap high-ranking security official in Haiti

The Caribbean islands battling the region's 'highest murder rate'

In an update on the situation in the Caribbean nation on Friday, Türk added that more than 50% of casualties occurred in the context of security operations against gangs, with hundreds struck "by stray bullets and explosive drones".

Gang violence had already been rampant under Moïse, but the power vacuum created by his murder allowed violent groups to seize more territory and become more influential.

Türk said gangs "continue to adapt and expand", with evidence collected by the UN pointing at "a strategy of seizing new territory and key transport routes, threatening stability".

The number of executions carried out by specialised police units dropped in recent months, he said, but people allegedly associated with gangs continue to face a high risk of summary executions.

The high commissioner added that recruitment of children into gangs has "nearly tripled", as to many minors joining a gang "can be the only mean of survival".

"No child should be forced to choose between their lives and the security of their neighbours," Türk said.

Haiti is preparing to hold its first presidential and legislative election since 2016 on 13 December.

However, Türk said that it is "hard to imagine the conditions to hold a credible election could be met this year", given the current situation.

A multinational police force has been operating in Haiti since 2025 to to tackle escalating gang violence in the conflict-torn country but it has struggled to even enter areas where gangs hold sway.

articles.title: Ex-Royal Marine from Dorset completes Pacific and Indian Ocean row
articles.summary: Dave "Dinger" Bell arrives in Kenya after setting off from Peru nearly 11 months ago.
articles.body:
A former Royal Marine has completed a solo and unsupported row across the Pacific and Indian Ocean, having not set foot on land for 327 days.

Dave "Dinger" Bell, from Bere Regis, Dorset, set off from the west coast of Peru on 9 November last year with 350 days worth of food and equipment on board his carbon-fibre boat.

He stepped ashore in Kilifi, north of Mombasa, Kenya, at 10:15 BST (12:15 local time) after rowing more than 15,000 nautical miles (28,000km).

He is using the trip to raise money for Rock2Recovery, a charity helping veterans and blue light workers suffering from PTSD.

On arrival in Kilifi, Bell stooped to touch the sand and was supported by his partner, Georgie, as he walked unsteadily up the beach where he was handed a beer.

Speaking to journalists in front of a waiting crowd, he said: "The last week has been so amazing. I've been the calmest I've ever been in my life.

"I've not stepped off that boat since the ninth of November. This is the first time I've touched land."

Bell, who arrived earlier than expected, said he still had enough food on board to last another 20 days.

When asked if he had seen any sharks, he said: "Yes, the most enjoyable part was the wildlife encounters I had.

"I was followed for weeks - one whitetip on one side and one on the other - and I would row for days like that."

In a video update on Monday, Bell said his head was just "monkey-braining around" between looking forward to being home and the practicality and logistics of being ashore.

He said: "The plan is for me to step off... go back to the hotel to clean up, sleep and rest and socialise with the people that are coming to see me, then come back to the boat - when I've got rid of my land legs hopefully, so I can walk by myself.

"I'm trying to second guess what it's going to feel like, trying to sensitise myself because It's going to be bewildering to step off and step on dry land - total sensory overload.

"I'm looking forward to it, it'll be a novelty to feel like that and it'll eventually wear off."

In 2021, Bell rowed across the Atlantic, from New York to Newlyn, Cornwall, and vowed never to do anything like it again.

But advances in technology, such as lighter boats, improved solar panels and autopilot systems made him curious about what else he could achieve.

He said he had avoided "clockwatching" by listening to podcasts and audiobooks, as well as by sending and receiving voicenotes.

In one, sent to BBC Radio Solent and recorded in the Indian Ocean, he said he had embarked on the challenge due to an "overwhelming sense of curiosity", adding: "The idea struck me it might be achievable and I couldn't let that go."

Bell's record-breaking journey took him in a westerly direction across the Pacific, the Coral Sea, Great Barrier Reef, Torres Straight and the north coast of Australia, before crossing the Indian Ocean.

He said his biggest challenge during almost 11 months at sea had been to "stop rowing" for eight weeks while crossing the South Pacific to avoid arriving in the Coral Sea during cyclone season.

"I was too quick so I had to slow down," he said.

"To sit, mid-ocean, knowing you've still got seven, eight, nine months at sea but not be rowing was one of the hardest things, psychologically, that I've ever had to deal with."

Among those congratulating Bell on his achievement on social media was TV adventurer Jason Fox who said: "He's done. Two oceans on his own. It is incredible. What he's done is insane and it's all for Rock 2 Recovery."

In a video post, former footballer and pundit Graeme Souness said: "Dave, I can't get my head around 15,500 miles. Truly, truly incredible. Well done you."

Bell's challenge has so far raised more than £110,000 for Rock2Recovery.

articles.title: Paid for 10 weight-loss sessions but attended only 4: How woman still won Rs 86,200 from wellness clinic
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A Tamil Nadu district consumer commission has directed a wellness clinic to refund Rs 51,200 to a woman who paid for a 10 session cryotherapy
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A Tamil Nadu district consumer commission has directed a wellness clinic to refund Rs 51,200 to a woman who paid for a 10 session cryotherapy package but attended only four sessions. The commission also awarded her Rs 25,000 for mental agony and inconvenience and Rs 10,000 as litigation costs. The order was passed on September 22, 2026.Why did the woman approach the consumer commission?According to the commission order, S Mayadevi saw an advertisement for weight reduction on social media and was contacted by staff of VeCura Wellness Clinic, who allegedly gave her assurances about the programme. She approached its Trichy branch in October 2024 and later opted for a 10 session cryotherapy package.The complainant paid Rs 51,200 towards the programme and also took loans through Bajaj Finance and EZFINANZ for payments connected with the treatment. She attended four sessions and alleged that she developed cold, running nose and fever during the treatment and that the clinic did not respond properly to her complaints. She also alleged that she gained weight instead of losing it.Mayadevi alleged that the clinic had promised 100 percent weight reduction and its advertisements amounted to an unfair trade practice. She sought a refund, compensation for mental agony and other relief.What did the consumer commission find?The bench comprising President T Sekar and member K Velumani noted that the clinic had admitted that the complainant opted for the 10 session package and attended four sessions. However, it had not produced treatment records, session reports, progress or weight charts, pre- or post-treatment assessments, consent forms or treatment protocols to show what services were provided.The commission added that the clinic could not simply retain the entire amount when a substantial part of the package remained unused.“The first opposite party was required to establish the nature and extent of services rendered and the basis for retaining the amount received,” the bench said.It, however, did not accept all allegations raised by the complainant. The commission said the advertisement containing the alleged 100 percent guarantee had not been produced. It also said there were no medical records establishing that her cold, running nose and fever were directly caused by the cryotherapy treatment.The commission then noted that the weight reduction cannot necessarily be treated as a guaranteed result because it can depend on lifestyle, compliance and physiological factors. But the clinic was still required to provide the service covered by the package for which it had received payment.“The first opposite party has failed to establish satisfactory performance of the paid service package and has failed to justify retention of the amount paid for the service which remained incomplete. Such failure amounts to deficiency in service under Section 2(11) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019,” the commission further added.The commission held that Mayadevi had established deficiency in service against VeCura Wellness Clinic. It dismissed the complaint against Bajaj Finance and EZFINANZ, saying their role as financiers did not by itself make them responsible for the clinic's service.The clinic was directed to:Refund Rs 51,200 received towards the cryotherapy package.Pay Rs 25,000 as compensation for mental agony and hardship.Pay Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs.Make the payment within 45 days of receiving the order.If the refund and compensation are not paid within that period, those amounts will carry 9 percent annual interest from the date of the order until payment.The commission therefore partly allowed the complaint against the clinic while dismissing the claims against the two finance companies. The order was pronounced on September 22, 2026.

articles.title: Dubai calls, Rs 1cr demand, planned firing: Goldy Brar-linked extortion racket busted; 3 held
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police has busted an alleged India-Dubai extortion network linked to the Goldy Brar gang and arrested three operatives, foiling a plan to
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police has busted an alleged India-Dubai extortion network linked to the Goldy Brar gang and arrested three operatives, foiling a plan to open fire at the residence of a Delhi businessman, news agency PTI reported citing officials said on Friday.The accused allegedly contacted businessman Praveen Jain through a UAE-based number on September 16 and demanded Rs 1 crore, while threatening his family with dire consequences. The caller allegedly claimed to be associated with gangster Goldy Brar.Jain received three missed calls around 8.15pm, following which his son Ayush received a call from the UAE number at around 9.27pm. A case was registered at Roop Nagar police station on September 17.Police said analysis of the communication trail showed that the calls were routed through virtual private server and data-centre infrastructure linked to the UAE.The investigation led police to Aarif alias Pistol, 32, who allegedly acted as a link between the Dubai-based callers and their associates in India. He was arrested from Ahmedabad's Vejalpur on September 24 with Gujarat Police's assistance.According to police, Aarif allegedly paid a Dubai-based associate, Aarish, to make the extortion call and instructed him to speak in Haryanvi to make it appear that the threat came from a local criminal.Police subsequently arrested Mubarik alias Gullu from Delhi on September 25. He allegedly helped plan the extortion attempt and arranged accommodation in Kirari for shooters who were to carry out the threat if the demand was not met.Police said intelligence inputs later indicated that the accused planned to fire multiple rounds at Jain's Roop Nagar residence and then repeat the extortion demand. Preventive arrangements were made at the house, foiling the alleged attack.During the probe, police found that the same UAE number was allegedly used to target another Delhi businessman in Rohini. On September 19, the younger brother of a construction businessman received two WhatsApp calls and a 37-second audio message from the number.The caller allegedly identified himself as Vikrant from Mahendergarh, claimed affiliation with the Goldy Brar gang and demanded Rs 1 crore within 48 hours, threatening firing and other consequences. A separate case was registered at Vijay Vihar police station on September 24.Police said four suspected shooters, two from Panipat and two from Khalapar in Muzaffarnagar, had allegedly been engaged to execute the threats. One of them, Nawab Ali alias Sonij, was apprehended on October 1 from a moving train near Rewari with the assistance of the Railway Protection Force, police said.Police said Aarif has been named in 12 cases registered between 2016 and 2026 at Kairana police station in Shamli, including cases related to attempt to murder, extortion, criminal intimidation, rioting and Arms Act offences.Police are now looking for the remaining accused and the Dubai-based caller. Investigators are examining communication records, digital evidence and financial transactions to establish the wider network and determine whether the group was involved in other extortion cases.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Containerabad’: Pakistan’s capital and truckers bleed money amid lockdown
articles.summary: As Islamabad prepares for another opposition march, drivers and businesses are counting the cost of the barricades.
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan — Two boys scale the rusted corner of a shipping container marked “EVERGREEN” in block white letters. They kick up into handstands, legs steady, without so much as a glance upward, even as traffic passes on the road behind them.

The clip runs 27 seconds, cut exactly to a verse from rap singer Cheema Y’s Punjabi track “Police”, about containers of smuggled goods crossing the border that nobody can account for.

The four-tonne container beneath their feet carries nothing at all. It is one of what transport associations and officials put at between 1,500 and 2,000 heavy steel boxes barricading Islamabad’s roads ahead of an opposition march.

The idea for the video, shared on Instagram six days ago, was the brainchild of 26-year-old Mujaddad Asrar, a callisthenics and parkour athlete. Asrar has been staging shoots like this one on Islamabad’s containers for several years. This clip, along with several others, went out from a friend’s account rather than his own, because the friend has a bigger following, he says.

“It’s like clockwork every year,” he told Al Jazeera. “One lot of containers or another comes right on time, like it’s part of the calendar. It’s basically a fifth season.

“Yeah, these containers have now made Islamabad as Containerabad,” he added, cheerfully.

The containers have been up for nearly four weeks as part of efforts by the country’s government to block an upcoming march on the capital by Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), the party of jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan. The party had planned to set off on September 27 from Peshawar, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, then pushed the date back to October 4, citing “strategic reasons.” The march is PTI’s latest attempt to pressure the government into releasing Khan, the country’s most popular political figure according to polls, who has been behind bars for more than three years.

Islamabad has been here before several times in recent years. In August 2024, as PTI petitioned the Islamabad High Court over a cancelled rally permit at D-Chowk, the square where the city’s high-security Red Zone starts, then-Chief Justice Aamer Farooq remarked that the authorities had turned the capital into a “container city”.

Talal Chaudhry, the state minister for interior, however, said the use of containers ahead of the coming protest reflects standard practice rather than overreach.

“Security preparations are based on intelligence assessments and anticipated security requirements, not simply on the date a political event is formally announced,” he told Al Jazeera. “Islamabad is the federal capital, so precautionary security arrangements are often put in place well in advance.”

The containers come with a price tag, though no one agrees on what it is.

Islamabad police initially sought roughly 820 million rupees ($2.9m) for a week of security arrangements around PTI’s planned march, according to local media reports. With the march delayed a week, officials now expect the final bill to top 1 billion rupees ($3.6m).

Container rental sits at the centre of that budget: one estimate puts the daily rental for more than 1,500 containers at 46.5 million rupees ($167,000).

While owners maintain they have not been paid for their containers, Chaudhry disputes this.

“What I can say with certainty is that legitimate container rentals are documented and paid through the proper process,” he said.

In a written reply to the National Assembly in March 2025, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi disclosed that the government had spent 1.35 billion rupees ($4.9m) on law-and-order deployments in Islamabad over five years, with a peak of 724 million rupees ($2.6m) in 2022-23.

The reply itemised personnel movement, housing and meals for deployed police, and, in one year, anti-riot equipment, but excluded the period covering the 2024 PTI protest. Nowhere in the government response did the word “container” appear.

Chaudhry rejected the idea that this amounted to an omission. “Container rentals are not necessarily recorded as a separate political-protest expenditure category,” he said. “They are processed through the established administrative and contractual mechanism. Every container hired is recorded, and the corresponding payment is traceable through official accounts.”

The containers fall into two categories: trucks with containers welded on to them owned by individuals, and containers owned by foreign shipping lines sitting on someone else’s vehicle.

Roughly 2,000 vehicles and containers are held across Islamabad, Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, according to transporters’ associations, though the figure remains an estimate rather than a definitive number.

Muhammad Owais Chaudhry, a lawyer who heads the All Pakistan Goods Transport Owners Association, represents owners in the first category — those whose trucks and containers have been grabbed by the police.

“If you combine the container and the vehicle, the total cost comes to 30,000 to 40,000 rupees ($108 to $144) a day,” he told Al Jazeera, describing earnings lost per truck-container combination while idle.

“Not a single rupee has been given,” he said of compensation from the government. “No procedure has ever been worked out for how it would be paid. In our history, no transporter has ever received money for any past protests.”

Talal Chaudhry, the state minister, disputes this entirely.

“That is simply not consistent with our records,” he told Al Jazeera. “Containers are hired through a proper contractual mechanism at market rates, and payments are made through official accounts. We have a complete container-by-container record, including payments made in previous years. If there is any legitimate outstanding claim, it will be settled.”

Owais Chaudhry has also pressed officials to buy a fleet of containers outright rather than renting them for every sit-in, adding that the purchase cost of a container is between 400,000 and 500,000 rupees ($1,444 to $1805).

Talal Chaudhry called that a question of policy, not principle.

“The government already has an established rental mechanism that allows containers to be deployed when required without permanently bearing the cost of purchasing, storing and maintaining them,” he said.

One of the vehicles seized belongs to Haji Atlas Khan, provincial general secretary of the All-Pakhtunkhwa Goods Federation.

He was at home in Nowshera district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province when his driver rang one evening in early September to say police had impounded his lorry minutes after it entered Islamabad.

“We didn’t know, and the police didn’t know either, under what authority these vehicles were being seized,” Khan told Al Jazeera.

In the following days, three more of his trucks joined the first at police stations across the capital.

Owais Chaudhry has watched containers seized for sit-ins and protests since 2018, he says. Haji Atlas Khan, in his early 50s, has been in the business for 26 years and has seen his vehicles impounded through several protests and rallies.

But neither has ever waited this long to retrieve a vehicle — and both insist they have never been paid for their losses.

Owais said association officials have met Islamabad’s police leadership and Talal Chaudhry since the crackdown began, but came out of those meetings with “empty promises”.

“Everyone says you’ll get everything,” he said. “But we ask, how, and when?”

Asked about a compensation timeline, minister Talal Chaudhry said the process concerns “the hiring or temporary use of containers, not an indefinite seizure of vehicles”.

Loaded vehicles, he said, were returned immediately, while empty containers taken for security arrangements fall under “the rental arrangement,” with release “coordinated with the relevant authorities.”

None of the drivers or transporters Al Jazeera spoke to recognised that arrangement, received anything in writing, or knew when they might get their vehicles back.

The container ownership has another variable, say sector experts.

“In most cases, the shipping line is the owner of the container,” Mehmood ul Hassan Awan, a Karachi-based customs agent and importer, told Al Jazeera. “We don’t have a single shipping line in Pakistan, only shipping agents.”

Of the roughly 2,000 containers stuck in the three regions, most, he says, belong to foreign shipping lines, each accruing $150 to $300 a day in penalties that flow abroad through the State Bank.

“Those dollars don’t come into our economy,” he said. “They go out.”

Drivers waiting for release tell a similar story. Owners don’t trust that their trucks and containers will stay safe even in police custody, so they ask drivers to stay near the vehicles — even as they gather dust parked on the streets of Islamabad.

On a strip of open ground near Islamabad’s fruit and vegetable market, Muhammad Naseer and a handful of others sit out the days on a mat laid beside their parked trucks.

Naseer, 48, from Mianwali, on the border of Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, was hauling an empty container back towards Karachi when police stopped him as he was leaving Islamabad.

“Our container belongs to a shipping line,” he told Al Jazeera. There is a 10-day window to return it, Nasir said, after which “a claim will come.”

One of the trucks nearby belongs to Khan from Nowshera district.

Muhammad Saleem Jaffar, his driver, recalled the night it was stopped: 3am, at a checkpoint near a wholesale market in Islamabad.

He had just dropped off his shipment when police stopped him. Like the others, he, too, has not been told when he might leave.

“No one has ever asked how we are,” he said of the police who come and go from the holding area. “Whether anyone of us is sick, what the loss has been. No one has asked anything at all.”

Driver Farooq Khan, 22, said the single washroom at a nearby fuel pump now draws an hour-long queue, and there has been nowhere to bathe since his container was seized.

The uncertainty extends to when it all ends.

Jaffar said a fellow driver walked to the nearby police post to ask about release, and was first told October 4. Days later, the police told him the date was changed to October 16, with no guarantee attached, he said.

“It could go beyond that too,” Jaffar said.

Asked if he had ever thought about simply walking away from the job, Naseer pointed first to the truck he was minding, worth close to 15 million rupees ($54,000) and entrusted to him by an owner in Karachi.

But he framed it as more than a question of money or debt.

“How can we become disloyal to him, and abandon the vehicle over a little hardship?” he asked.

Back in the city where Asrar and his friends perform atop the containers, the economics take a different shape.

The full cost, says Sajid Amin Javed, deputy executive director for research at the Sustainable Development Policy Institute, goes well beyond container rental.

“When we close a hotel and cancel all bookings, it is not the room rent that the hotel loses,” he told Al Jazeera. “It is the signalling it sends to investors, businesses, tourists. Every pillar of state, society bears that cost.”

The impact is not limited to the capital, others say.

“The metropolitan area it forms with Rawalpindi is the third-largest in the country,” said Danyal Adam Khan, an Islamabad-based researcher and urban governance specialist, adding that people from distant provinces too were deeply integrated into the socioeconomic fabric of the city. “When you shut down the capital like this, you cut everyone off.”

For now, the containers remain where they have always ended up: half barricade, half backdrop, and Asrar says the response to his friends’ video online has mostly been good-natured.

“Some people call it showing off,” he said. “Some call it political. We try to stay neutral about it.”

Asrar recalled one police officer who figured they were not damaging anything and stayed to watch. “They were just impressed by it,” he added, speaking of his stunts.

But not everyone has the luxury of treating the containers as a backdrop.

“This is such a government that it doesn’t listen to anyone’s request, anyone’s plea, anyone’s complaint,” Khan, the truck owner, told Al Jazeera. “There’s simply no one we can go to who will hear us.”

articles.title: Ex-England cricket star Botham joins Dales wind farm protest
articles.summary: Former England player Lord Botham opposes plans for 23 wind turbines near the Yorkshire Dales.
articles.body:
Former England cricketer Lord Ian Botham is set to join a protest walk against plans for a wind farm on moorland near the Yorkshire Dales.

Campaigners opposing the proposed Hope Moor development on land between Arkengarthdale and Teesdale say 23 turbines more than 656ft (200m) high would harm a nationally important landscape.

Developer Fred. Olsen Renewables argues the scheme could generate enough renewable electricity to power about 135,000 homes while helping meet climate targets.

Lord Botham, who lives near Richmond, is due to take part in a walk across Barningham Moor organised by opponents on 11 October.

Campaigners have previously condemned the development as the "devastating industrialisation" of Yorkshire Dales moorland.

Organisers of the Walk for Hope Moor said the event would give people the chance to experience the "scale, tranquillity and beauty" of the moorland while raising awareness of their campaign.

Tim Wilson, from the Hope Moor Wind Farm Action Group, said Lord Botham's support could help bring national attention to local concerns.

He said: "More than six million people visit these areas and the wind farm would have a massive impact in terms of enjoyment, amenity and the reasons people come here.

"We've had very good local support and awareness, but we're hoping an iconic figure like Lord Botham, who has a passion for wildlife and the countryside, will help take the campaign to a national level and into Westminster."

Lord Botham is among several prominent figures who have backed opposition to the scheme.

Earlier this year, mountaineer Alan Hinkes OBE described the proposal as "the right development in the wrong place".

According to the Local Democracy Reporting Service , Fred. Olsen Renewables said the site had been chosen because of its strong and consistent wind speeds and could make an important contribution to reducing carbon emissions and improving energy security.

The company said further environmental assessments would seek to avoid sensitive areas, minimise impacts on wildlife and identify opportunities for peatland restoration.

It has also encouraged residents, businesses and community groups to submit feedback as plans for the development continue to be refined.

articles.title: Barrow's regeneration plans including theatre and market unveiled
articles.summary: Plans for Barrow, Cumbria, are being consulted on, including a replacement theatre and market.
articles.body:
Plans to redevelop a town centre, that has been without a permanent market or theatre for two years, have been unveiled.

People in Barrow, Cumbria, are being consulted on plans for a new theatre venue, homes, retail and commercial space, public areas and parking provision.

Team Barrow, which is leading on the redevelopment project, said the plans were "concepts rather than final designs" and were intended to help people visualise what could be possible.

The town is set to undergo a 10-year regeneration project, with the first phase expected to cost about £23m. It follows plans to demolish Barrow's market hall and theatre over concerns about asbestos.

Consultations are being held until Saturday and would help "inform the next stages as the plans continue to be developed and refined", Team Barrow said.

Team Barrow's interim chief executive Andrew Bennett, said: "Some of you may be excited by what you see. Some of you may have concerns. Some of you may have challenging questions.

"That's absolutely okay. In fact, we welcome it."

Team Barrow said the plans responded to "long-held concerns and frustrations about the town centre".

Both The Forum and Market Hall shut in 2024 and are due to be demolished in 2028 .

Plans by the group were previously criticised for their lack of detail and the area's Labour MP Michelle Scrogham called for the project to be brought under " proper local control ".

Consultation events are being held at Barrow Town Hall from 11:00 BST to 19:00 and on Saturday 3 October at The Bridge on Portland Walk from 10:00 to 15:00, in partnership with Westmorland and Furness Council.
