articles.title: As Dishwashers take over more kitchens across India: Here are the dos and don'ts you should not miss
articles.summary: The dishwasher is a precision tool. Used right, it works well and lasts for years.
articles.body: The dishwasher is a precision tool. Used right, it works well and lasts for years. If not handled well, it gives poor results, spoils utensils, and needs early repairs. The stakes are higher for Indian households. You might need a cooker, a tadka pan and a serving bowl for a simple dal. If you have more than three people in the family, the pile grows fast, and so does the temptation to cram in two more things. That is what these rules are for.The wrong detergent, an overloaded rack or a cast-iron kadai can ruin a dishwasher's performance, and sometimes the machine itself. Here is what to do, what to avoid, and why each rule matters.Start with detergent, where most users go wrongDishwashers need dishwasher-specific detergent. Regular dishwashing liquid produces huge amounts of foam, which can overflow and damage the machine.Do use:Tablets or all-in-one podsDishwasher gel, liquid or powder, placed in the dispenser (never sprinkled loose)Rinse aid in its separate compartment, for streak-free dryingDishwasher salt, if you live in a hard-water areaNever use:Regular dishwashing liquidHand soap, body soap or laundry detergentBaking soda or vinegar as a routine wash (an occasional rinse is fine)More detergent than recommended, since extra soap leaves residue and does not clean betterIndustry voices say the same. Praveen Gusain, Vice-President & Business Head, Kitchen Products at LG says:"When using a dishwasher in an Indian kitchen, the right loading and care practices can make a significant difference to cleaning performance. Do scrape off large food particles before loading and arrange items such as oily kadhais, pressure cookers, plates and bowls so that water can reach all surfaces. Avoid overloading the racks or placing utensils in a way that blocks the spray arms. There is also no need to manually pre-wash and soak every dish, particularly when using a dishwasher with steam-cleaning capabilities.It is important to use dishwasher-specific detergent and, where applicable, dishwasher salt and rinse aid. This is particularly relevant in areas with hard water, where salt can help manage mineral build-up. Rinse aid can support better drying and help minimize water spots. Consumers should also regularly clean the filter and spray arms and leave the dishwasher door slightly open after a cycle to allow the interior to dry."Know what goes in and what stays outGetting this wrong is the fastest way to damage your utensils, so check before you load.Safe to wash:Stainless steel thalis, katoris and dabbasSingle-piece steel kadais and steel tawasMetal pressure cooker bodiesAll cutlery and ladlesGlasses, ceramic cups and heat-resistant glassMelamine plates (on a cool or normal cycle)Food-grade plastic marked PPNon-stick cookware with an intact coatingHand wash only:Cast iron kadais, tawas and cookwareCopper, brass and aluminium vesselsPressure cooker rubber gasketsScratched non-stickWooden ladles and spatulas, and items with wood or bone handlesCrystal glasswareTerracotta and clay potsThin plastic containers, which can warpLoad it smartlyHow you load matters as much as what you load. Water has to reach every surface, so every rule below is about letting it circulate.Scrape, don't rinse. Remove solid food and thick masala, then load. Pre-rinsing wastes water, time and detergent.Angle bowls and katoris face down, so they don't pool water.Load the kadai face down at an angle on the bottom rack.Stand thalis upright in the plate slots.Keep glasses inverted in the cup holders, and make sure they don't touch.Leave gaps so water can circulate. Packed racks mean poorly cleaned dishes.Check the spray arms spin freely before you start, and don't let any utensil block them.Keep large items off the top rack, and never place sharp knives point-up.Pick the right cycle, and read the energy labelMany people choose a short cycle to save water or electricity and then fill the machine to the top. The result is dishes that are hardly washed and need a second washing, so nothing is saved. Match the cycle to the soiling – heavier oily loads need the intensive or heavy-duty setting, but lightly soiled loads can use a faster cycle. Let the cycle do its job. The wash water is usually heated to about 120 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit, which helps to break down grease.When you buy or use a machine, look at its energy label. If it carries a BEE star rating, more stars indicate a more energy-efficient appliance, so compare ratings across models before you buy. For everyday loads, an eco-friendly cycle is usually the efficient choice, as long as the soiling is light. Keep the intensive setting for greasy kadais and cookers.The hard-water tip for Indian kitchensIf your city has hard water, as most cities in Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra do, use dishwasher salt in the salt compartment. Hard water leaves white mineral deposits on steel utensils. Salt softens the water inside the machine and prevents this. It is separate from detergent and needs a refill every few weeks.What it costs to run, compared with hand-washingA dishwasher uses less water than hand washing, and conserves energy and household labour. That is doubly important in an Indian home where cooking means many pots. The savings only come if you do full loads, don’t pre-rinse and don’t have to rewash because of overloading or the wrong cycle. An almost empty load wastes the water and power you were trying to save. Wait until the machine is full.There is also a cost that never shows up on a bill: the hours spent scrubbing oily utensils after every meal.Maintain it like any other applianceManufacturer guidance generally points to the following routine. Skipping it is the most common reason a good machine starts to underperform.Do:Clean filter every 2 to 4 weeksWipe door seals once a month with a damp clothRun an empty hot cycle with dishwasher cleaner monthly.Top up rinse aid monthly.Check the spray arm holes & remove clogs with a toothpickAfter a cycle, leave the door slightly open so the inside can dryDo not:Ignore the filter; clogs decrease cleaning efficiencyIf you have to open the door mid-cycleLeaving wet dishes sitting for hours after the cycle is finishedIgnore error codes. Look at the manual right now.The bottom lineMost dishwasher problems stem from the same few habits: the wrong soap, an overloaded rack, an item that should have been hand washed, and a filter that hasn't been cleaned. Fix those four and the machine can save hours of scrubbing every week for years to come.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Waterway fares fixed during Vikramshila Setu closure
articles.summary: Bhagalpur administration sets ferry and cargo fares during Vikramshila Setu closure till Dec 31; Rs 35 passengers, Rs 50 motorcycles, free for kids, bikes, ambulances.
articles.body: Bhagalpur: The Bhagalpur district administration has fixed rates for waterway ferries and cargo services during the closure of Vikramshila Setu till Dec 31. The services are aimed at easing movement between the two sides of the river. The rates were finalised after considering financial quotations and proposals received for operating ferries and cargo vessels.Nine agencies had submitted proposals, following which the rates were finalised by the district committee with vessel operators. The assessment was necessitated by the large number of people, including milkmen, banana and vegetable sellers, commuting between Naugachia and Bhagalpur daily.A consensus was reached on a fare of Rs 35 per passenger and Rs 50 per motorcycle. The vessel operator will not collect fares from passengers with payments to be made by the govt based on the number of passengers or the vessels’ carrying capacity. The service will be free for children below 12 years, bicycles and ambulances.The fare for three-wheelers has been fixed at Rs 150, loaded tractors at Rs 500 and unloaded tractors at Rs 250. Pickup vans will be charged Rs 600 when loaded and Rs 300 when unloaded, while four-wheelers will be charged Rs 700 and loaded 10-wheelers Rs 3,800. Twelve-wheelers, 14-wheelers, 16-wheelers and 18-wheelers will be charged Rs 4,400, Rs 4,500, Rs 4,800 and Rs 5,000 respectively.Seventy per cent of the fare will be paid to vessel operators as reimbursement, while 30% will be deposited under the relevant govt account head. articles.body: India's relationship with rice changes dramatically from one region to another. The grain appears in everyday meals, traditional recipes, festive dishes and local cuisines across the country.Among the many rice-growing regions, West Bengal is popularly known as the “Rice Capital of India.” The title reflects the state's long-standing connection with paddy cultivation and its distinctive rice-based food traditions.Why is West Bengal called the Rice Capital of India?West Bengal has a landscape particularly suited to paddy cultivation, with fertile plains, river systems and substantial rainfall supporting rice farming across several regions.Paddy cultivation has consequently become an important part of rural life in the state, with farmers growing different varieties suited to local conditions.The state's rice tradition also has a strong culinary identity, with bhaat, or cooked rice, forming the base of countless Bengali meals.Bengal has several traditional rice varietiesWest Bengal's rice heritage is not limited to one type of grain.Gobindobhog is a small-grained, aromatic variety widely associated with Bengali cuisine. Its fragrance and slightly sticky texture make it suitable for dishes such as khichuri and festive preparations.Tulaipanji, associated with North Bengal, is another traditional aromatic variety known for its distinctive flavour and texture.The state also has numerous local rice varieties that have developed through generations of cultivation in different agricultural regions.Rice appears in Bengali celebrationsRice is also closely connected with Bengali desserts and special-occasion cooking.Payesh, made with rice, milk and sugar, is traditionally prepared for birthdays and other celebrations. The dish is often associated with auspicious occasions and family gatherings.Rice flour is used in several Bengali preparations as well, including traditional sweets and delicacies prepared during festivals.The grain has shaped everyday Bengali mealsA traditional Bengali lunch can feature rice alongside dal, vegetables, fish and other accompaniments, with each dish adding a different flavour and texture to the meal.Fish and rice have become particularly associated with Bengali cuisine, reflected in the familiar cultural phrase “macher jhol, bhaat”, referring to fish curry served with rice.Different rice preparations are also chosen according to the dish, occasion and season, giving the grain a surprisingly varied role within Bengali cooking.Rice is celebrated differently across IndiaWest Bengal's rice traditions form just one part of India's much larger rice culture.In South India, rice is transformed into foods such as idli, dosa and curd rice, while eastern and northeastern regions have their own traditional preparations and varieties.Biryani, pulao, khichdi and lemon rice further show how the same grain can take on entirely different culinary identities.So, which state is known as the Rice Capital of India?West Bengal is popularly known as the Rice Capital of India.Its association with extensive paddy cultivation, distinctive rice varieties and a cuisine in which rice occupies a central place has given the state this widely recognised nickname.The title ultimately reflects something easy to understand: in Bengal, rice is not merely an ingredient. It is part of the region's agricultural history, traditional cooking and everyday food culture.Thumb image: Canva (for representative purposes only)Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Noah's Ark mystery enters new phase as researchers probe deep beneath site
articles.summary: In new developments, Noah's Ark researchers drilled over 60 feet into Turkey's Durupınar site and say they found no solid rock beneath the boat-shaped formation.
articles.body: Researchers investigating the site believed by some to be Noah's Ark have just wrapped up their first full field season — drilling more than 60 feet beneath the site and collecting hundreds of samples now undergoing laboratory analysis. The Noah's Ark Research Project, supported by Ağrı İbrahim Çeçen University, has spent the last year collecting soil samples at the Durupınar site near Mount Ararat in eastern Turkey. First identified in 1959, the boat-shaped formation has long drawn speculation over a possible connection to Noah's Ark, though geologists have argued it is a natural formation. HOLY LAND DISCOVERY REVEALS ANCIENT CHARRED RELICS FROM ONE OF JERUSALEM'S DARKEST CHAPTERS In a 1996 paper, geologists Lorence Gene Collins and David Franklin Fasold rejected claims that the formation was Noah's Ark, concluding instead that it was "a natural rock structure." But in the decades since, researchers have continued investigating the site, with a university-backed project now using deep-core drilling and other methods to probe beneath the formation. During the latest field season, researchers collected over 300 soil samples from varying depths inside and outside the formation, Noah's Ark Research Project vice president Andrew Jones told Fox News Digital. The team also used deep-core drilling at the site for the first time, reaching depths of 20 meters, or more than 60 feet, in some locations — and obtaining samples from within the formation that were sent for lab analysis. ARCHAEOLOGISTS MAKE UNUSUAL FIND NEAR SITE WHERE ARK OF THE COVENANT WAS ONCE KEPT "That's what we'll be testing this winter," Jones said. "Just to see if we can find any type of manmade activity or something that suggests decayed wood." The researchers hope the analysis will help determine whether there are signs of human activity or materials consistent with decayed wood beneath the formation. Jones said the decision to drill deeper followed earlier sampling in 2024 that showed differences between soil collected inside and outside the formation. Those samples, he said, contained three times more organic matter inside the site, along with 38% more potassium and differences in pH. "Near [the] surface, we're seeing a difference in the soil," Jones said of the earlier results. "Let's go deeper this year and see what we can find." LOST CITY TIED TO BIBLICAL EXODUS MAY HAVE FINALLY BEEN DISCOVERED IN EGYPT Any such evidence could be significant for the research team, which is investigating whether the boat-shaped formation could contain the remains of a man-made structure. Jones said the team believes its drilling results raise questions about some previous explanations of the site as a natural rock formation. "When we drilled into the formation this year for the first time, we did not encounter any solid block of rock, of limestone, [or] of any type of a rock," Jones said. "We were hitting mainly soil." Although the team encountered boulders in some locations, Jones said researchers did not find a consistent, solid block of rock beneath the formation. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "We’re still studying our results, but we believe that this should give [skeptics] pause when they say this is a rock formation," Jones said. "We still have the lab work to do." Ancient pottery discovered near the formation has also fueled renewed interest in the site, with some recent reports linking the fragments to the Noah's Ark theory. Jones, however, clarified that the pottery was found beside the formation, not within it. The pottery had been tentatively dated by its style from the early Chalcolithic, or Copper Age, through the Iron Age, he added. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Jones said there are two ancient settlements near the formation and suggested their proximity could be significant if the site were ultimately connected to Noah’s Ark. "You can connect the dots," Jones said, though he noted that the nearby settlement has not been excavated. "If this is Noah’s Ark, we have people living right beside it early on." Jones, who identified himself as a Christian, said he believes in the biblical story but cautioned that the team still has "a lot of work to do." He urged people not to jump to conclusions. He also said he understood why some remained skeptical of the project. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "I can understand because I have friends who are atheists or agnostic, and they think that I’m looking for Santa’s house or something," he said. The expert stressed that the team's field work was complete but that laboratory analysis was still underway before broader conclusions could be drawn. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We still have the lab work to do," Jones said. "And I hope everyone can follow along and see what we find."

articles.title: Stabbed, bleeding, still fighting: How hero Indian pilot helped stop another 9/11-type attack
articles.summary: This week, we are tracking: The 30-second plunge: How hero Indian pilot helped stop another 9/11-type attack From MAD to AI: Are Altman and Amodei the new
articles.body: This week, we are tracking:The 30-second plunge: How hero Indian pilot helped stop another 9/11-type attackFrom MAD to AI: Are Altman and Amodei the new keepers of Doomsday?MRP mystery: Who gets the money between factory and patient?Asian Games: A medal in many sports, a gold in too fewStabbed, bleeding, still fighting: How hero Indian pilot helped stop another 9/11-type attackAt about 34,000 feet over Saudi Arabia, flydubai flight FZ1073 was a routine Dubai-to-Tel Aviv service carrying 174 people on board. Then there was sudden mid-air action. The co-pilot stabbed the captain and tried to crash the aircraft.The Boeing 737 Max 8 dropped more than 14,000 feet in about 30 seconds, according to Flightradar24 data. A passenger, Naama Bershadski, said she closed her eyes, convinced “We are going to die”.In the cockpit, Captain Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, was badly wounded and lying on the floor. Israeli officials say he gathered what strength he had left to hit the door release.That gave passengers and crew a way in. They overpowered the co-pilot. Two other pilots, who were on board to operate the next flight, took control of the aircraft. The flight diverted to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely.A heroPraise for Machchhar came quickly. PM Modi called him a hero and said his courage saved hundreds of lives. “In the face of the gravest danger... he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others,” PM Modi wrote on X.Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu credited him with preventing a "catastrophic midair disaster."“The pilot, in bad shape, had the sense to open the door. In a way he was a hero,” US President Donald Trump said.‘Kill me, kill me’Netanyahu said that the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination”. He told Fox news that when restrained, the co-pilot cried “kill me, kill me”. The co-pilot, reported to be an Omani national, has not been named publicly yet.Read more:'I was reciting Hanuman Chalisa': flydubai 'hero' Captain Smit Machchhar tells PM Modi about cockpit orde'Consider for Ashoka Chakra': Milind Deora writes to PM Modi seeking honour for pilot Smit MachchharAirlines wake up to ‘insider threat’ after flydubai attackPM Modi speaks to 'hero' flydubai pilot Smit Machchaar, hears his account of the ordealThe world's Smit-ten: PM to Trump, praise pours in for braveheart pilotForget Trump and Xi. Altman and Amodei could decide humanity’s fateThe world thinks its future rests on Trump and Xi. It may come down to whether Sam Altman and Dario Amodei can stop hating each other.Since the US and erstwhile Soviet Union acquired nuclear weapons, humanity has lived with the possibility of annihilation: Mutually assured destruction, or MAD.Now, it’s the US and China. Donald Trump and Xi Jinping can escalate or ease a trade war, restrict or exchange technology, and decide whether the US and China cooperate on the risks of artificial intelligence.But the more consequential rivalry may be unfolding below the level of presidents. It is between Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic.The pace is set by a personal feud. Amodei left OpenAI in 2020 convinced that Altman was a manipulator who could not be trusted with AGI. As Kevin Roose recounts in the Atlantic, Amodei has written in internal messages that Altman and OpenAI are "evil". However, some at OpenAI regard Amodei as a power-hungry virtue-signaller.The danger in the Altman-Amodei rivalry is not that they are reckless by temperament. It is that the feud has turned caution into a competitive liability.The worst scenario is a mutual misread. One lab, convinced its rival is about to leap ahead, releases early or trims a safety test. The other sees this and does the same. Nobody planned for catastrophe, and everybody can explain their own step as defensive. A hotline between Washington and Beijing won't help if the trigger is pulled in San Francisco, because by the time a model misbehaves in the wild, the decisions that mattered were already made.Read more:Less than a week after Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit, the US government rules out working with China on AI; the American President says: Do not want ...As AI fears ‘spread’, Donald Trump to meet CEOs of Meta, Google, Nvidia, Anthropic and other tech companies$1tn at stake & unbridled power: Amodei, Altman & Musk fear AI could doom humanity but Trump & China can’t seem to stop race - why?Bombs without brakes? Why the US-China AI race may be harder to control than the nuclear one'Let's race, not wrestle': 5 takeaways as Trump-Xi navigate trade, Taiwan and AIRs 2,700 to Rs 27,000: Inside the strange economics of India's medicine pricesOn September 22, the Supreme Court asked why an essential cancer drug that retailers buy for about Rs 2,700 can carry an MRP of Rs 27,000. A week later, a bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta called the tenfold markup "carnage" and asked why the 16% retail margin used in price-control rules could not cap MRP over the price to retailer.The SC also noted that inflated MRPs can also end up being reimbursed under government-funded health schemes. In that situation, the margin is not merely being paid by a desperate patient. It is being paid by the taxpayer.The Centre acknowledged that excessive pricing was a problem and said it would consult officials to find a solution. The case returns on October 12.The MRP questionWho keeps the difference between the price the pharmacy pays and the price printed on the strip. A pharmacy’s purchase price is not the factory’s manufacturing cost, which is rarely public. The printed MRP is a maximum selling price. The manufacturer, marketer and distributors earn their shares before the strip reaches the pharmacy.Why simply capping MRP may not solve everythingIf regulators merely cut the printed MRP but leave incentives throughout the chain untouched, manufacturers, distributors, hospitals and retailers can reorganise margins elsewhere.The question is no longer merely how cheaply India can make a medicine.It is why an inexpensive medicine can become so expensive by the time a sick Indian is asked to pay for it.Read more:Kerala High Court expands Union government’s power to intervene in pricing of patented drugs'Broad daylight dacoity': SC questions overpricing of essential cancer drugsIndia accounts for 20% of world’s childhood cancers: JipmerIndia's Asian Games: Plenty of medals, not enough goldIndia's medal count at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games is healthy, but the gold count is a worry.Through October 2, India has 75 medals (15 gold, 25 silver, 35 bronze), good for fifth place.Gold problemIndia finished fourth at Hangzhou with a record 107 medals, including 28 gold. Of those golds, 20 have already slipped away.What’s nextA strong finish would make this a better campaign. But the broader assessment is already coming into focus: We can win medals in many sports, but we need more athletes and teams to take the final step to gold.Read more:Sujeet Kalkal wins India's first wrestling gold at Asian Games 2026Three golds in a day! articles.body: Tata Sons, which sits at the centre of the Tata Group and owns stakes in companies ranging from Tata Consultancy Services and Tata Motors to Air India and Jaguar Land Rover, is facing one of the worst boardroom disputes in its 158-year history.The company’s leadership is now openly split with its largest shareholder Tata Trusts – an umbrella group of charitable trusts that collectively own about 66% stake in Tata Sons – over key decisions. Two of those trusts, Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) and Sir Ratan Tata Trust (SRTT), together hold about 51.5% stake.

articles.title: Hindutva is Bhartiyata and Hindustaniat - it is the living essence and expression of the non-partisan, all encompassing Hindu Dharma
articles.summary: The applause that Smit Machchhar, the Captain of the FlyDubai flight got for saving the passengers on board and preventing a reportedly catastrophic
articles.body: The applause that Smit Machchhar, the Captain of the FlyDubai flight got for saving the passengers on board and preventing a reportedly catastrophic international terror incident is a reflection of the on-going Indian Renaissance. His conversation with the Prime Minister, Shri Narendra Modi today on a Video Call, wherein he articulated his thoughts and actions after being fatally stabbed by his co-pilot, reflect the essence of the core values that his culture and religion inculcated in him. His valour in saving others even in the face of death, is nothing but a natural reiteration of always being the protector and never the aggressor, as underlined in our scriptures, epics and ballads over millennia. This incident should serve as an eye opener to all those who are paranoid of our assertions of identity.The composite cultural renaissance that is finding expression in Bhartiyata, Hindustaniat or Indianness has unnerved many. Most of all, an entitled, elitist and now dethroned political oligarchy, which is suffering from acute paranoia. This paranoia emanates out of fear of a people- a civilisation waking up, after decades of ideological slumber, forced upon them by the ruling elite of a newly independent India.This renaissance, loosely termed as Hindutva Bhartiyata or Hindustaniat has irked many with vested interests to make baseless, indeed unsavoury statements. Left-leaning scholars and cosmopolitan voices have repeatedly argued that Hindutva contradicts India's constitutional secularism, failing to grasp that dharma transcends narrow religious categories. It is a philosophical claim about the nature of an ancient civilisation, which is an oxymoron. Such a claim cannot be answered with slogans or counter slogans. It must be met with texts, ideas, jurisprudence, and the long memory of a civilisation that has reflected on power, restraint, and duty for over three millennia. It is this civilizational memory engrained culturally in the Indian psyche that was at display when the pilot of the FlyDubai flight endangered his life to save the life of others. These others were neither his relatives nor compatriots. They were fellow human beings.Tragically, the proponents of anti Hindutva/Bhartiyata/Hindustaniat rhetoric are those, who are themselves deeply entrenched in dogma and convolutedly, define the Hindu, Bauddh and Jain Dharmas in terms of dogmatic “isms”. These “isms” applicable to political and economic theories like Marxism-Leninism-Maoism-Naxalism, Liberalism, Socialism and Conservatism etc, are being blatantly misused to define civilizationally evolved ancient faiths and religions. For this methodically devious class of people, while the practice of the Christian faith is Christianity & practice of the Muslim faith is Islam, the practice of Hindu, Bauddh and Jain faith are, Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism. Suffice to say that such people deliberately, or in their informed ignorance, do not understand that our Dharmas- Religions, find expression in their essence- the tatva.Hinduism has never been a faith confined to belief or ritual alone. It has never rested on dogma or depended on a single theological proposition or a book. It is dharma - a comprehensive framework governing conduct, ethics, social harmony, and the pursuit of truth. Former President of India, Dr S Radhakrishnan repeatedly reminded us that, Hinduism is not a religion in the narrow sense but a way of life, a spiritual discipline that accommodates plurality without surrendering moral coherence. Hindutva emerges from this civilizational self-understanding. It is not fear dressed as identity. It is continuity asserting itself in history.To separate Hinduism from Hindutva is to misunderstand both. Hinduism is the civilizational source and Hindutva is the civilizational consciousness and its expression. While the former provides metaphysical depth, the latter provides cultural articulation. They are not opposites. They are expressions of the same dharmic worldview, responding to different historical moments.Our foundational texts leave little room for caricature. The Manusmriti, frequently invoked, but rarely read with seriousness, begins not with hierarchy but with universal ethical restraint. Manu defines the core of dharma thus:Ahimsa satyam asteyam shaucham indriya nigrahahEtam samasikam dharmam chaturvarnye abravin manuhNon-violence, truth, non-stealing, purity, and control of the senses are the guiding principles of Bharat and the Hindu Dharma. Manu explicitly declares these as, samasika dharma, i.e. universal duties applicable to all human beings, irrespective of social station. Sarvajana Narayan’s classical commentary clarifies, that these virtues are enjoined upon all people, not merely the four varnas. Yajnavalkya reinforces this view, when he states, that virtue itself is the means of happiness for all. This is not paranoia. This is moral universalism.The Bhagavad Gita deepens this ethical architecture. Lord Krishna enumerates the divine qualities in language that leaves no ambiguity:Ahimsa satyam akrodhas tyagah shantir apaisunamDaya bhutesv aloluptvam mardavam hrir achapalamTejah kshama dhritih shaucham adroho natimanitaBhavanti sampadam daivim abhijatasya BharataHarmlessness. Truthfulness. Freedom from anger. Compassion towards all beings. Absence of greed. Modesty. Steadiness. Forbearance. Purity. Absence of pride. These are the marks of, one born to a divine disposition. A civilisation that elevates such qualities as ideals, cannot be reduced to fear or insecurity.Even war, the harshest of human enterprises, is governed by ethical law in Hindu thought. Manu’s instructions on warfare are among the most striking moral texts in world literature. He states:Na cha hanyat sthalarudham na klibam na kritanjalimNa muktakesham nasinam na tavasmiti vadinamNa suptam na visannaham na nagnam na nirayudhamNayudhyamanam pashyantam na parena samagatamNayudhavyasanapraptam nartam natiparikshatamNa bhitam na paravrittam satam dharmam anusmaranA warrior must not kill one who is dismounted, helpless, supplicating, wounded, terrified, asleep, disarmed, naked, surrendering, or turning away. Even in the midst of battle, Manu insists, that one must “remember the dharma of the good.” Victory achieved through wanton cruelty is no victory at all. This is not paranoia. It is ethical restraint elevated to law.India of the Hindu Dharma has lived and practiced these values in continuity through millennia. From the ancient examples of rectitude in battles between Porus and Alexander to those between Huns and our indigenous rulers, from Kshamadan of Munshi Prem Chand to as recent as the 1971 Indo-Pak War that led to liberation of Bangladesh, ours is an ongoing civilization that finds no parallel. The 1971 War resulted in about hundred thousand, Pakistani ‘Prisoners of War’, held captive in India. We could have used them as leverage or killed them, however, in another expression, the Hindu civilizational values, we not only treated them with dignity, but returned them to a reluctant Pakistan with all humility.The Ramayana and the Mahabharata return to this moral vision repeatedly. Heroes are defined not by conquest but by fidelity to duty. Rama relinquishes power to uphold Dharma. Yudhishthira refuses falsehood even at the cost of defeat. Bhishma chooses suffering over dishonour. These are not romantic myths. They are civilizational pedagogy of the ancient Hindu civilization. They teach that moral order matters more than success.Hindutva flows from this ethical universe. It is not a theological doctrine. It is not a claim of religious supremacy. It is the assertion, that this civilizational ethic, shaped by centuries of reflection on duty, restraint, and compassion, has the right to endure and to express itself without apology.Even the traditional understanding of the word Hindu dissolves the charge of paranoia. Classical derivations explain Hindu as one who rejects what is low and sinful, or one who feels pain at the suffering of others. One derivation traces it to hin, meaning hinsa or harm, and du, meaning distance. A Hindu is one who distances himself from harm to others. Another derivation suggests one who feels pain at the pain of others and cruelty is therefore, not merely social failure but civilizational betrayal.The Bhagavatam reinforces this moral demand with striking clarity. It declares that God does not accept the worship of one who harbours hatred toward living beings, even if the rituals are performed with perfection. Love and goodwill toward all creatures are declared the highest form of devotion. Without this, worship is hollow.It is these Hindu values that find expression in,“Sarve Bhavantu Sukhinah, Sarve Santu Niramaya,Sarve Bhadrani Pashyantu, Ma Kaschid Dukh Bhag Bhavet”Vasudhaiv Kutumbakam - the whole world as a family, is another expression of timeless Hindu thought.Tulsi Das distils this worldview in a single couplet that captures the spirit of Hindu civilization and its overarching ability to tolerate, co-exist, absorb and assimilate:Tulsi ih sansar mein bhanti bhanti ke logSabson hil mil chaliye nadi naav sanjogThis world contains people of many kinds. Live in harmony with all. Human association is as brief as a shared boat journey. This is not sentimentalism. It is civilizational wisdom.Political order, too, is framed as a moral necessity, in Hindu thought. The king exists not for domination but for the prevention of chaos. Without lawful authority, society descends into insecurity, where the strong prey upon the weak. Loyalty to just rule is therefore presented as a dharmic duty, essential for social stability and the pursuit of virtue.When modern thinkers articulated Hindutva, they were not inventing a new religion. They were naming this civilizational consciousness, in the language of their time. Swami Vivekanand and Dr Radhakrishnan themselves argued repeatedly, that Hinduism survives because it is flexible yet rooted, adaptive yet continuous. Hindutva, in this sense, is Hinduism aware of itself in history.The Supreme Court of India recognised this reality when it described Hindutva as a way of life rather than a religious dogma. In doing so, law acknowledged what philosophy had long understood. We have to understand and appreciate that a civilizational ethic, cannot be reduced to narrow theological categories.To dismiss Hindutva as paranoia is to mistake self-awareness for insecurity. It amounts to judging a civilization by political noise rather than by its moral foundations. Hindutva is not fear of difference or plurality. To term it as paranoia of the Hindu religion, is refusal to forget inheritance. Hindutva is not aggression. It is continuity.Hindutva is Hinduism, conscious of its civilizational journey. Rooted. Ethical. Enduring. And civilisations that have taught restraint even in moments of power do not survive through fear. They survive through memory and ever continuing rectitude. Hindutva as the practice and expression of Hindu faith does not need to be apologetic. It has for thousands of years faced many attacks aimed at annihilating it. The evidence of history demonstrates that Hindutva, far from weakening under sustained assault, has grown organically stronger as Indians reclaim their dharmic heritage - a civilizational awakening that Prime Minister Narendra Modi has articulated to the world. Hindutva is nothing but that all encompassing and all assimilating majestic river, that Guru Rabindranath Tagore described as Bharat Tirtha - a pilgrimage that embraced even its destructors as its own.The author is the Lieutenant Governor of LadakhDisclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: Italy's underwater marble sculptures were built as art; a study finds they are becoming small artificial reef habitats
articles.summary: Five marble statues stand on the seabed of the Baia del Cannone, off Talamone in Grosseto, Tuscany, in the Northern Tyrrhenian Sea.
articles.body: Five marble statues stand on the seabed of the Baia del Cannone, off Talamone in Grosseto, Tuscany, in the Northern Tyrrhenian Sea. They were placed there on 19 September 2024 as part of an initiative run by the association Casa dei Pesci. According to the study published in the MDPI journal titled ‘Early Biodiversity Responses to Underwater Marble Sculptures Deployed as Artificial Reefs: First Scientific Assessment of a Conservation Initiative in the Northern Tyrrhenian Sea’, underwater installations were conceived primarily to enhance habitat heterogeneity, support conservation outreach and promote community engagement. What the authors call the "first systematic scientific assessment" of an art-based marine conservation initiative. Researchers from the University of Siena and partner organisations monitored the site for one year.How are Italy’s underwater marble sculptures becoming artificial reefsAccording to the authors, Mediterranean coastal ecosystems are affected by habitat degradation and loss of structural complexity. The pressures they list include climate change, coastal development, pollution, overexploitation and destructive fishing practices. In the Talamone area, additional local pressures include episodes of illegal bottom trawling. Casa dei Pesci, a non-profit association, has deployed concrete anti-trawling blocks along the coast to deter that activity. The paper states that the marble sculptures serve a different primary function: habitat enrichment, biodiversity enhancement and environmental awareness.The bay already hosted two marble sculptures, deployed at greater depth in 2016. A further 22 underwater marble sculptures lie beneath the Rocca di Talamone and in front of the "Bagno delle Donne", and together these installations form the local underwater museum. Earlier artistic deployments in the bay were not monitored systematically, so the new work establishes a quantitative ecological baseline. The research was funded by the European Social Fund Plus 2021–2027 under the Giovanisì programme of Regione Toscana, within the project VESPESCA.How did scientists monitor Italy’s underwater marble sculpturesThe five monitored sculptures are S1, "Cimitero senza nome"; S2, "Guardiano"; S3, "Sigillo"; S4, "Genesi"; and S5, "Porta per gli abissi". According to the study, each was carved from a marble block with an approximate initial weight of 12 tonnes. They were deployed from a pontoon with the help of scuba divers and arranged in two rows, approximately 7 metres from each other. The site lies at 5.5–6.5 metres depth on soft-bottom habitat, selected to be free of Posidonia oceanica meadows.Surveys took place on 19 September 2024, then on 4 March, 19 June, 7 August and 18 October 2025. At each visit, the team laid three 20-metre transects and collected five 50 × 50 cm photoquadrats along each. Fish were counted within 3 metres on either side of every transect line, a surveyed area of 120 square metres per transect. Divers also inspected each sculpture for two minutes, covering exposed surfaces and the underside, and recorded the taxa they saw as presence-only data. Underwater visibility during the surveys ranged from 3 to 7 metres.What marine life is colonising Italy’s underwater marble sculpturesThe authors write that the qualitative surveys on the sculptures offered the most direct indication of ecological change linked to the intervention. Community composition differed according to both survey date and microhabitat, with exposed surfaces and sheltered undersides following different trajectories. On exposed surfaces, Padina pavonica, Balanus perforatus, Sertularella sp., Cratena peregrina and Arbacia lixula had become more frequent by October 2025. The study notes that the joint appearance of hydroids and the nudibranch C. peregrina suggests the surface had begun to support early trophic relationships. Sculpture S1 showed the largest increase on exposed surfaces, rising from 4 taxa in March 2025 to 15 in October 2025.Undersides changed more slowly. Their turnover was lower and driven mainly by the cardinalfish Apogon imberbis and the sea cucumber Holothuria poli. The authors point out that A. imberbis is closely associated with shaded cavities and sheltered microhabitats, and they read its later presence as a sign that the undersides had become suitable as refuge habitat. The difference between surface and underside was weak at the first post-deployment survey and became stronger from June 2025 onward. The maximum richness recorded on undersides in October 2025 was 6 taxa.How did fish assemblages change around the underwater marble sculpturesTotal fish abundance, species richness and Shannon diversity did not differ significantly among survey dates, according to the study. Assemblage composition did. The silverside Atherina hepsetus contributed most to the difference between the deployment survey and March 2025, being present at deployment and absent in March. By October 2025, the assemblage was characterised by higher abundances or the appearance of Coris julis, Diplodus vulgaris, Sarpa salpa, Mullus barbatus and Serranus scriba. On the surrounding seabed, photoquadrats showed turf, Caulerpa prolifera, bare substrate and Posidonia oceanica as the dominant components, with limited temporal change. The authors report that the sculptures did not produce detectable short-term changes in the composition of the surrounding benthic cover.The authors describe the work as a pilot-scale assessment, covering only the first year after deployment at a single site with three transects and no independent control area. They state that survey date covaries with season and time since deployment, so the fish pattern cannot be read as a response to the sculptures alone. Fish size was not recorded, and large schools were estimated visually. The paper adds that artificial reefs may also generate ecological trade-offs, including the facilitation of non-indigenous species, and that longer-term monitoring is required. articles.title: Six snake charmers held from train for collecting money
articles.summary: RPF arrested six snake charmers on Amritsar-Purnia Janseva Express after RailMadad alert for soliciting money with snakes; reptiles handed to forest dept.
articles.body: Patna: Railway Protection Force (RPF) arrested six snake charmers for allegedly collecting money from passengers by displaying snakes in the general coach of Amritsar-Purnia Court Janseva Express (14618) on Friday.ECR chief public relations officer (CPRO) Saraswati Chandra said the incident came to light after Sonepur RPF received a message through ‘RailMadad’ regarding the presence of snake charmers in the train and their activities of seeking money from passengers by showing them snakes. Taking the complaint seriously, RPF personnel coordinated an operation to apprehend them, he said.RPF sub-inspector Shamsher Kumar and assistant sub-inspector Vijay Kumar found the six snake charmers moving through the general coach and collecting money from passengers by displaying snakes.As soon as the train reached Dighwara under Sonepur division of ECR around 10.45 am, the RPF personnel arrested all six persons and deboarded them from the train for questioning. During questioning, they kept changing their statements about their identities and places of residence. They sometimes claimed to be from Lucknow or Himachal Pradesh, raising further doubts about their antecedents, CPRO said.“Carrying snakes on trains and using them to solicit money from passengers is not permitted. articles.title: New free repair shop to launch in Jericho area of Oxford
articles.summary: Organisers hope the initiative will attract enough interest to continue on a monthly basis.
articles.body:
Free help with repairing bikes, electrical items, computers and clothes is coming to an Oxford neighbourhood.

On Saturday, the first Jericho Repair Shop will take place at St Barnabas CE Primary School, in Jericho, between 10 and 12:00 BST.

Organiser John Mair said everyone was welcome to come along and donations would go back into rental costs and advertising for the event, which he hoped would continue on a monthly basis.

He said an initiative such as the repair shop "stops people throwing things away".

Mair said he decided to start a repair shop in Jericho after having used the service himself.

"I went to the repair shop in Wolvercote maybe a year or two ago and they repaired my garden blower - I thought this is a good idea," he said.

"I've brought over the man who repairs bicycles in Wolvercote, people who repair sewing, people who do computers, who sharpen knives."

Co-ordinator of Share Oxford, which also runs repair cafes in Oxford, Ben Tuppen previously said society needed to be more innovative in its approach to sustainability.

"If it doesn't work, repair it, don't throw it away and certainly don't throw it on the pavement," Mair said.

Listen to the latest news from Oxfordshire

Mair said he was looking forward to the launch and expected "anywhere between 10 and 100 people".

"It costs you nothing, but we'll expect a donation," he said.

"If enough people turn up, it'll be the first Saturday of November, and if enough people turn up, first Saturday of December."

Mair, who has been organising public events in Jericho such as Lazy Saturday and Lazy Sunday in Mount Place , said he wanted to see "how much demand there is".

He added: "All communities need hubs and this might as well be one, so why not?"

articles.title: Black metal band Venom's frontman Cronos dies aged 63
articles.summary: Newcastle rock giants Venom describe Conrad Cronos Lant as "fearless and unmistakable".
articles.body:
The co-founder, frontman and ever-present bass player of pioneering heavy metal band Venom has died at the age of 63, it has been announced.

For almost 50 years Conrad Lant, known by his stage name Cronos, led the Newcastle band credited with inventing the black metal genre and cited as a major influence by thrash metal bands including Metallica, Slayer and Anthrax.

In a tribute, the group said Lant's "voice, bass and vision were at the heart of Venom" and described their bandmate as "uncompromising, fearless and unmistakable".

His son Nathan thanked the band's fans down the decades "for all of the support you have given my dad over the years, I know he really appreciated you all".

Venom began in Newcastle in 1978, formed by musicians from three other bands, but it was their second album - Black Metal released in 1982 - that cemented their status in the rock world.

Playing a fast style mixed with Lant's dark imagery and lyrics, the album gave its name to an entire subgenre and influenced bands on both sides of the Atlantic.

Speaking to BBC Newcastle, rock journalist Simon Rushworth said: "They were massively influential [and] spawned a whole genre of what I'd call extreme metal.

"The likes of Slayer, Metallica, Anthrax, they all cited Venom.

"Venom took Metallica out on the road in the mid-80s before anybody knew who they were. Then Metallica returned the favour and took Venom on the road with them.

"Cronos was right at the heart of it, not only with the music.

"He was the one who brought a lot of the early artwork to the table and kind of created this black metal image."

That imagery brought the band to the attention of the US government when the band's track Possessed was included on the "Filthy Fifteen" list of songs compiled by the Parents Music Resource Center, the committee behind the adoption of "parental advisory" warning stickers.

The original line-up began to break apart following Possessed and Cronos pursued solo projects until a short-lived and acrimonious reunion in the mid-90s.

With changing line-ups, but still led by Cronos, Venom continued to the present day, releasing a 14th studio album - Into Oblivion - this year.

In a tribute on social media, original guitarist Jeff "Mantas" Dunn said: "Despite the turbulent history of this band, it was at the end of the day the three of us, who started something so special and changed the direction, the movement and the history of metal as we know it.

"At times like this the thing I remember is the friendship that we had in those early days, that one for all, all for one mentality, that rebellious quality and the absolute driven urge to be something so different whether it was accepted or not."

Rushmore said the band were themselves influenced by the likes of Motorhead, Kiss, Black Sabbath and Alice Cooper, adding: "Cronos wanted Venom to be a more evil and flamboyant hybrid of all of those bands.
